metadata.title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space
metadata.authors: Tomas Mikolov, Kai Chen, Greg Corrado, Jeffrey Dean

nodes.name: Computational complexity of a model
nodes.statement: Computational complexity of a model is defined as the number of parameters that need to be accessed to fully train the model.
nodes.statement_clean: A model's computational complexity equals the total parameter accesses during training.

nodes.name: Total training complexity
nodes.statement: Training complexity is proportional to $O = E \times T \times Q$, where $E$ is number of training epochs, $T$ is number of words in the training set and $Q$ is the per-example complexity for the architecture.

nodes.name: 1-of-$V$ word encoding
nodes.statement: Each input word is encoded as a one-hot vector over the vocabulary of size $V$.

nodes.name: Hierarchical softmax with Huffman binary tree
nodes.statement: Vocabulary is represented as a Huffman binary tree assigning short codes to frequent words; the number of evaluated output units reduces to about $\log_2(\mathrm{Unigram\_perplexity}(V))$ instead of $V$.

nodes.name: Word relationship question
nodes.statement: A question is a pair of word pairs sharing the same relationship; e.g. ``what is to $small$ as $biggest$ is to $big$?''. It is answered by the nearest word to $X = vector(\text{biggest}) - vector(\text{big}) + vector(\text{small})$ under cosine distance.

nodes.name: Semantic-Syntactic Word Relationship test set
nodes.statement: A test set with 5 semantic categories (8869 questions) and 9 syntactic categories (10675 questions), formed by pairing manually-written word pairs and requiring an exact match of the predicted nearest word.

nodes.name: Feedforward Neural Net Language Model (NNLM)
nodes.statement: Probabilistic feedforward neural network with input, projection, hidden and output layers; jointly learns word vectors and a statistical language model.
output: Probability distribution over the next word
Learned word vectors (rows of the shared projection matrix)

nodes.name: Recurrent Neural Net Language Model (RNNLM)
nodes.statement: Recurrent neural network language model with input, hidden, and output layers connected via time-delayed recurrent connections in the hidden layer; word representations have the same dimensionality $D = H$ as the hidden layer.
output: Probability distribution over the next word

nodes.name: Continuous Bag-of-Words Model (CBOW)
nodes.statement: Log-linear classifier that predicts the current (middle) word from the average of projections of $N$ context words (4 history + 4 future), with no non-linear hidden layer and a hierarchical-softmax output.
input: Context size $N$ (e.g. 8: four future + four history)

nodes.name: Continuous Skip-gram Model
nodes.statement: Log-linear classifier that, given the current word, predicts surrounding words within distance $C$; the actual range $R$ is sampled uniformly in $\langle 1; C \rangle$ to weight nearby words more.

nodes.name: DistBelief parallel training with Adagrad
nodes.statement: Distributed framework that runs multiple model replicas in parallel; each synchronizes gradient updates through a centralized parameter server using mini-batch asynchronous SGD with the Adagrad adaptive learning rate.
nodes.origin_citation: Dean et al. 2012 (DistBelief); Duchi et al. 2011 (Adagrad)

nodes.name: Word-offset analogy solver
nodes.statement: Given an analogy ``$a:b :: c:?$'', compute $X = vector(b) - vector(a) + vector(c)$ and return $\arg\min_w \cos(\mathrm{vector}(w), X)$ over the vocabulary, excluding the input words.

nodes.name: Skip-gram sentence completion scoring
nodes.statement: For each candidate sentence, place the unknown word at the input of a trained Skip-gram model, predict every surrounding word, and score the sentence by the sum of these per-position log-probabilities; choose the highest-scoring candidate.

nodes.name: Look up context word vectors
nodes.statement: For each of the $N=8$ context words (four before, four after the target), retrieve its row from the shared input projection matrix.

nodes.name: Average context vectors
nodes.statement: Average the $N$ retrieved context vectors into a single projection vector (the projection layer is shared across positions, so word order does not matter).

nodes.name: Predict middle word with hierarchical softmax
nodes.statement: Feed the averaged vector into a log-linear classifier whose output is computed via hierarchical softmax over the Huffman tree, predicting the middle word.

nodes.name: SGD update
nodes.statement: Update both the input projection matrix and the hierarchical-softmax weights via stochastic gradient descent with backpropagation; learning rate starts at $0.025$ and decays linearly to zero.

nodes.name: Sample context window radius
nodes.statement: For the current word, draw $R$ uniformly from $\langle 1; C \rangle$ (with $C=10$ in the experiments) so that distant words contribute fewer training examples.

nodes.name: Form $2R$ (input, output) training pairs
nodes.statement: For each of the $R$ words before and $R$ words after the current word, form a training example with the current word as input and that surrounding word as the target label.

nodes.name: Predict targets with hierarchical softmax
nodes.statement: For each (input, output) pair, project the input word and predict the target word with a log-linear classifier through the hierarchical softmax.

nodes.name: SGD update
nodes.statement: Update the projection and softmax-tree parameters via SGD with linearly-decayed learning rate.

nodes.name: Compute analogy vector
nodes.statement: Compute $X = vector(b) - vector(a) + vector(c)$.

nodes.name: Nearest-neighbour search
nodes.statement: Return $\arg\min_{w \notin \{a,b,c\}} \cos(\mathrm{vector}(w), X)$ over the full vocabulary; mark correct only on exact match.

nodes.name: Total training complexity
nodes.statement: $O = E \times T \times Q$

nodes.name: NNLM per-example complexity
nodes.statement: $Q = N \times D + N \times D \times H + H \times V$, with hierarchical softmax reducing $H \times V$ to $H \times \log_2 V$, leaving $N \times D \times H$ as the dominant term.

nodes.name: RNNLM per-example complexity
nodes.statement: $Q = H \times H + H \times V$, dominated by $H \times H$ once $H \times V$ is reduced to $H \times \log_2 V$ by hierarchical softmax.

nodes.name: CBOW per-example complexity
nodes.statement: $Q = N \times D + D \times \log_2 V$.

nodes.name: Skip-gram per-example complexity
nodes.statement: $Q = C \times (D + D \times \log_2 V)$, where $C$ is the maximum word distance.

nodes.name: Time-constrained word-vector estimation
nodes.statement: Choose model architecture, vector dimensionality $D$, vocabulary size and corpus size $T$ to maximize accuracy on the Semantic-Syntactic Word Relationship test set under a fixed training-time budget.

nodes.name: Microsoft Research Sentence Completion Challenge
nodes.statement: Given 1040 sentences each with one missing word and five candidate words, select the most coherent completion. Prior state of the art was 55.4\% (combination of RNNLMs).

nodes.name: Hidden layer dominates NNLM cost
nodes.statement: Most of the per-example complexity in feedforward and recurrent NNLMs is caused by the non-linear hidden layer (the $N \times D \times H$ or $H \times H$ term).
assumptions: Hierarchical softmax applied to reduce the $H \times V$ output term
conclusions: Removing the hidden layer is the key lever for training on much larger corpora at fixed compute

nodes.name: Word vectors encode multiple degrees of similarity
nodes.statement: Trained word vectors carry not only nearest-neighbor similarity but also algebraic regularities, e.g. $vector(\text{King}) - vector(\text{Man}) + vector(\text{Woman}) \approx vector(\text{Queen})$.
assumptions: High-quality word vectors trained on large data
conclusions: Many syntactic and semantic regularities are linear in vector space

nodes.name: Joint scaling of dimensionality and data
nodes.statement: Adding more training data or more vector dimensions alone yields diminishing returns; both must be increased together. Doubling either roughly doubles training cost (eq.~\ref{eq1}).
assumptions: Fixed vocabulary (30k most-frequent words for the calibration table)
conclusions: Practical recipe: scale $D$ and $T$ jointly rather than one at a time

nodes.name: Skip-gram dominates on semantic analogies
nodes.statement: On 640-dim vectors trained on the same 320M-word corpus, Skip-gram reaches 55\% semantic accuracy versus 24\% (CBOW), 23\% (NNLM), 9\% (RNNLM); CBOW leads on syntactic (64\%).
assumptions: Same corpus and dimensionality across architectures
conclusions: Skip-gram is preferable when semantic regularities matter most; CBOW when syntactic matter most

nodes.name: One-epoch training on 2x data matches three-epoch training
nodes.statement: Training a model for one epoch on twice as much data gives comparable or better accuracy than three epochs on the original data, with additional speedup.
conclusions: Single-pass training on more data is preferable to multi-epoch training on less

nodes.name: DistBelief Skip-gram sets new state of the art
nodes.statement: Trained with DistBelief on 6B words at 1000 dimensions, Skip-gram reaches 65.6\% total accuracy (66.1\% semantic, 65.1\% syntactic) vs CBOW 63.7\% and NNLM 50.8\%.
conclusions: High-dimensional Skip-gram + large data + distributed training yields the best published accuracy

nodes.name: Skip-gram + RNNLM sets new MSR Sentence Completion state of the art
nodes.statement: A weighted combination of Skip-gram (48.0\% alone) with RNNLMs reaches 58.9\% accuracy on the MSR Sentence Completion Challenge, beating the prior best of 55.4\%.
assumptions: 640-dim Skip-gram trained on the 50M-word MSRSCC corpus
conclusions: Skip-gram scores are complementary to RNNLM scores

nodes.name: King -- Man + Woman $\approx$ Queen
nodes.statement: $vector(\text{King}) - vector(\text{Man}) + vector(\text{Woman})$ is closest to $vector(\text{Queen})$ in cosine distance, illustrating semantic linear regularity.

nodes.name: biggest -- big + small $\approx$ smallest
nodes.statement: Computing $vector(\text{biggest}) - vector(\text{big}) + vector(\text{small})$ and taking the cosine-nearest word recovers $smallest$ when vectors are well-trained.

nodes.name: Country--capital and other relationship table
nodes.statement: Skip-gram (300-dim, 783M words) recovers analogies like $Paris - France + Italy = Rome$, $Einstein - scientist \to Messi: midfielder$, $copper - Cu \to zinc: Zn$, etc., across capitals, currencies, comparatives, and named-entity professions.

nodes.name: Out-of-the-list word selection
nodes.statement: Given a list of words, compute the average vector and pick the most distant word as the outlier; observed to give good accuracy, a popular human-IQ-test format.

nodes.name: CBOW dimensionality vs data sweep (Table 2)
nodes.statement: Accuracy on the 30k-vocabulary subset of the test set, sweeping $D \in \{50,100,300,600\}$ against $T \in \{24M, 49M, 98M, 196M, 391M, 783M\}$, shows diminishing returns from scaling either factor alone.

nodes.name: Same-data architecture comparison (Table 3)
nodes.statement: On 320M-word LDC corpus with 640-dim vectors: RNNLM 9/36/35, NNLM 23/53/47, CBOW 24/64/61, Skip-gram 55/59/56 (Semantic / Syntactic / MSR Word Relatedness).

nodes.name: Public-vector comparison (Table 4)
nodes.statement: Compares Collobert-Weston, Turian, Mnih, Mikolov-RNNLM, Huang public vectors with the authors' NNLM, CBOW, Skip-gram on the full Semantic-Syntactic test set; Skip-gram (300d, 783M) reaches the best 53.3\% total.

nodes.name: Epoch-vs-data study (Table 5)
nodes.statement: 1-epoch CBOW/Skip-gram on 1.6B words match or beat 3-epoch on 783M words at lower wall-clock cost.

nodes.name: DistBelief 6B-word training (Table 6)
nodes.statement: NNLM 100d 14$\times$180 CPU-days reaches 50.8\%; CBOW 1000d 2$\times$140 reaches 63.7\%; Skip-gram 1000d 2.5$\times$125 reaches 65.6\% on the test set.

nodes.name: MSR Sentence Completion results (Table 7)
nodes.statement: 4-gram 39\%, LSA 49\%, log-bilinear 54.8\%, RNNLMs 55.4\%, Skip-gram 48.0\%, Skip-gram+RNNLMs $\mathbf{58.9}$\%.

nodes.name: Huffman tree speedup is modest for NNLM, crucial for hidden-layer-free models
nodes.statement: Huffman-tree hierarchical softmax shrinks output evaluation from $\log_2 V$ to $\log_2(\mathrm{Unigram\_perplexity}(V))$, roughly $2\times$ on a 1M vocabulary; not crucial for NNLM (bottleneck is $N \times D \times H$) but essential for the new shallow models.

nodes.name: Multiple example averaging improves analogy accuracy
nodes.statement: Averaging the relationship vector across 10 example pairs (instead of one) lifts semantic-syntactic accuracy by about 10 percentage points absolutely on the best models.

nodes.name: Follow-up: open-source word2vec
nodes.statement: After the initial draft, the authors released multi-threaded C++ code at \url{https://code.google.com/p/word2vec/} achieving billions of words/hour on a single machine, plus 1.4M named-entity vectors trained on 100B words.
